draft.title: Appraising performance
card: Appraising performance means judging how well an athlete or team performed, then using that judgement to plan the next phase of training.
Video
lets coaches and athletes replay and slow down technique or tactics, so they can spot faults that are hard to see live.
Statistics
give measurable data, such as times, scores or distance covered. Comparing them across games or sessions shows trends.
Feedback
is information from a coach, teammate or the athlete about what went well and what to change. It adds views that numbers and footage may miss.
draft.remember: Gather evidence, judge the performance, then use it to plan the next phase of training.

a.q: Why does a coach compare an athlete's statistics across several games?
opts: To show trends that can guide the next training phase
To remove the need for any feedback from the athlete
To prove that the athlete's technique is already perfect
To choose the supplements the athlete should be taking
a.why: Data from several games shows whether results are improving or slipping, so the coach can plan what to train next. Statistics do not replace feedback, because feedback adds views that numbers may miss.
a.clue: Think about what a pattern over time tells a coach.

b.q: Priya, a netball shooter in Perth, scores well, but her coach thinks her footwork is poor before she shoots. Which method would best let them check this?
opts: Slow motion video of her footwork before each shot
Her total goals scored across the season
A count of how many games her team has won
Her own rating of how tired she felt after games
b.why: Video can be replayed and slowed down, so it shows exactly what her feet are doing before the shot. Goal totals are tempting, but they show results and not how she moves, so they cannot show a footwork fault.
b.clue: Which method shows how she moves, not just the result?

a.best: To show trends that can guide the next training phase

b.best: Slow motion video of her footwork before each shot

proposal.title: Appraising performance
card: Appraising performance means judging how well an athlete or team performed, then using that judgement to plan the next phase of training.
Video
lets coaches and athletes replay and slow down technique or tactics, so they can spot faults that are hard to see live.
Statistics
give measurable data, such as times, scores or distance covered. Comparing them across games shows trends, but they show results, not how a skill was done.
Feedback
is information from a coach, teammate or the athlete about what went well and what to change. It adds views that numbers and footage may miss.
proposal.remember: Gather evidence, judge the performance, then use it to plan the next phase of training.

a.q: A coach's statistics show a striker's shots on target have fallen over five games. What is the best next step in appraising performance?
opts: Use the trend to adjust the next phase of training
Keep the training plan the same until the season ends
Judge the striker on the most recent game alone
Rely on the statistics and ignore the striker's views
a.why: Appraisal means using the judgement to plan the next phase of training, so the falling trend should shape what is trained next. Judging on one game is tempting, but it throws away the trend that several games reveal. Ignoring the striker's views also misses what feedback can add.
a.clue: What is the judgement for, once it has been made?

b.q: Priya, a netball shooter in Perth, scores well, but her coach suspects a fault in how she lands just before she shoots. Which method would best let them check this?
opts: Slowed-down video replays from her recent games
Her shooting percentage recorded in each game
Her goal attack's comments straight after each game
Her own rating of how well she shot in each game
b.why: A landing fault is a quick movement that is hard to see live, and video can be replayed and slowed down to show it. Shooting percentage is tempting, but statistics show results, not how she moved. Comments after the game rely on what was seen live, so they may miss the fault.
b.clue: Which method lets you watch a fast movement again?
